en: Thus have I heard— The Discourse on the Great Mass of Suffering (Mahādukkhakkhandhasutta), the Thirteenth in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī;
what if we were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?
Then those bhikkhus went to the park where the wanderers of other sects resided; having arrived, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the bhikkhus:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama proclaims the full understanding of sensual pleasures, and we too proclaim the full understanding of sensual pleasures.
Friends, the ascetic Gotama proclaims the full understanding of forms, and we too proclaim the full understanding of forms."
"Friend, the ascetic Gotama proclaims the full understanding of feelings, and we too proclaim the full understanding of feelings.
In this regard, friend, what is the distinction, what is the difference in meaning, what is the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us—
namely, in the teaching of the Dhamma or in the instruction?"
Then those bhikkhus neither rejoiced in the speech of those wanderers of other sects nor rejected it;
without rejoicing and without rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed, thinking:
"We shall understand the meaning of this speech in the presence of the Blessed One."
Then those bhikkhus, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, returned from their almsround after the meal and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, venerable sir, having dressed ourselves in the morning and taken our bowls and robes, we entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then, venerable sir, this thought occurred to us:
‘It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī.’”
"What if we were now to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?
Then, venerable sir, we went to the park where the wanderers of other sects resided. Having arrived, we exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects;
and when we had concluded our polite and friendly conversation, we sat down to one side. As we were sitting there to one side, venerable sir, those wanderers of other sects said this to us:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too teach the full understanding of sensual pleasures.
Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of forms; we too teach the full understanding of forms.
Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the full understanding of feelings; we too teach the full understanding of feelings."

"Friends, what is the distinction here, what is the difference, what is the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us, namely, in his teaching of the Dhamma compared to our teaching of the Dhamma, or in his instruction compared to our instruction?
Then, venerable sir, we neither rejoiced in the speech of those wanderers of other sects nor did we reject it;
without rejoicing and without rejecting, we rose from our seats and departed.
‘We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.
Monks, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
‘But, friends, what is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, and what is the escape?’”
"What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, and what is the escape?
When asked this, monks, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and they will fall into further distress.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that is outside one's domain.
Monks, I do not see anyone in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins... [who could refute it].
In this world with its devas and humans, who else— apart from a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or having heard it from such a person— could satisfy the mind by answering these questions?
And what, monks, is the gratification in sensual pleasures?
"Monks, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.
What five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust."
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … flavors cognizable by the tongue …
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust— these, monks, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure— this, monks, is the gratification in sensual pleasures.
And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in sensual pleasures?
Here, bhikkhus, a clansman earns his living by some craft or trade—whether by accounting, calculation, or reckoning;
whether by agriculture, commerce, or cattle-rearing; whether by archery, government service, or any other craft whatsoever.
“Bhikkhus, being vexed by cold, vexed by heat, afflicted by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things,

and oppressed by hunger and thirst— even this, bhikkhus, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, having sensual pleasure itself as its cause. Yet, bhikkhus,
if those possessions do not come to fruition for that clansman despite his thus exerting himself, striving, and making an effort...”
Thus he sorrows, grows weary, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion, thinking:
"Vain indeed has been my exertion; fruitless indeed has been my effort.

Monks, this too is a visible danger in sensual pleasures, this mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
If, monks, those riches are successfully acquired by that clansman as he thus exerts himself,
strives, and makes an effort, he experiences pain and grief on account of guarding them,
thinking: "How can it be that kings do not carry off my riches, nor thieves steal them, nor fire burn them, nor water sweep them away, nor unloved heirs take them?"
While he is thus guarding and protecting those possessions, kings may seize them, or thieves may steal them, or fire may burn them, or water may carry them away, or unloved heirs may take them.
He sorrows, suffers, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion, thinking:
"What was mine is no longer mine."

“Monks, this too is a visible danger in sensual pleasures: a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its very cause.

Furthermore, monks, because of sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as their very cause, kings quarrel with kings, kshatriyas quarrel with kshatriyas, and brahmins quarrel with brahmins.”
Householders dispute with householders; a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother;
a father disputes with his son, and a son disputes with his father;
a brother disputes with a brother, a brother disputes with a sister, and a sister disputes with a brother; even a friend disputes with a friend.
There, having fallen into quarrels, disputes, and contention, they attack one another with their hands, they attack with clods of earth, they attack with sticks, and they attack with weapons.
There they undergo even death or suffering amounting to death.

This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures; it is a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, rooted in sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the source, and sensual pleasure as the basis— precisely because of sensual pleasures—
they take up sword and shield, fasten on their bows and quivers, and charge into a battle arrayed on both sides, while arrows are being shot,
spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing.
There they are pierced by spears, pierced by javelins, and their heads are cut off with swords.
There they undergo death, or suffering amounting to death.

This too, bhikkhus, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures; this mass of suffering has sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its source, sensual pleasure as its basis, and sensual pleasure itself as its reason.
Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, and sensual pleasures as the basis— precisely because of sensual pleasures—
men take up sword and shield, fasten on their bows and quivers, and charge forward into battle amidst the clashing of shields,
while arrows are being hurled, spears are being cast, and swords are flashing.
There they are pierced by spears, pierced by javelins, drenched with boiling cow dung, crushed under heavy logs, and their heads are cut off with swords.
There they undergo death itself, or suffering equal to death.

This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures; it is a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
Furthermore, monks, for the sake of sensual pleasures, with sensual pleasures as the cause, with sensual pleasures as the basis, and with sensual pleasures alone as the reason,
people cut through embankments, carry off plunder, commit burglary, lie in ambush on highways, and go to another's wife.
When kings have seized such a person, they subject them to various forms of punishment.
They beat them with whips, they beat them with canes, they beat them with clubs;
they cut off their hands, they cut off their feet, they cut off both hands and feet; they cut off their ears, they cut off their noses, they cut off both ears and noses;
they subject them to the "boiling oil" torture, they subject them to the "conch-shell-shaven" torture, and they subject them to the "Rāhu’s mouth" torture.
They perform the *jotimālika* penance; they perform the *hatthapajjotika* penance; they perform the *erakavattika* penance;
they perform the *cīrakavāsika* penance; they perform the *eṇeyyaka* penance; they perform the *baḷisamaṁsika* penance; they perform the *kahāpaṇika* penance;
they perform the *khārāpatacchika* penance; they perform the *palighaparivattika* penance; and they perform the *palālapīṭhaka* penance.
They do so; they douse them with boiling oil, have them devoured by dogs, impale them alive on stakes, and cut off their heads with swords.
There they undergo even death, or suffering equal to death.

This too, monks, is a visible danger in sensual pleasures: this mass of suffering has sensual pleasures as its cause, sensual pleasures as its source, sensual pleasures as its basis, and has sensual pleasures alone as its cause.

Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as cause, sensual pleasures as source, sensual pleasures as basis, and with sensual pleasures alone as cause, they engage in misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, and misconduct by mind.

Having engaged in misconduct by body, having engaged in misconduct by speech, and having engaged in misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

This too, bhikkhus, is a danger regarding sensual pleasures pertaining to the future—a mass of suffering caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, conditioned by sensual pleasures, and having sensual pleasures as its very cause.
And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from sensual pleasures?
“Monks, the removal of desire and lust for sensual pleasures, the abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—
this is the escape from sensual pleasures. For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the gratification of sensual pleasures as gratification,
the danger of sensual pleasures as danger, and the escape from sensual pleasures as escape— they will surely [not escape] sensual pleasures by themselves.”
"Or that they will cause another to fully understand it, so that by practicing accordingly one might fully understand sensual pleasures—
this is impossible. But those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who understand sensual pleasures as they really are— in terms of gratification as gratification,
in terms of danger as danger, and in terms of escape as escape— they will indeed [understand them] for themselves."
Or they will fully understand sensual pleasures, or they will encourage another to do so, such that by practicing accordingly one will fully understand sensual pleasures—this is possible.
And what, monks, is the gratification in forms?
It is like a maiden of the kṣatriya, brahmin, or householder class who is fifteen years of age.
Or sixteen years of age, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair— was that, monks,
at that time the supreme beauty of complexion?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Monks, whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on beauty and the appearance of color—
that is the gratification in forms.
And what, monks, is the danger in forms?”
In this case, monks, one might see that same sister at a later time,
eighty, ninety, or a hundred years of age, decrepit, bent like a roof-rafter, hunched, leaning on a staff,
trembling as she walks, afflicted, her youth gone, with broken teeth, grey hair, bald and shorn, wrinkled, and her body covered in age spots.
“What do you think, monks?
Has that former beautiful appearance vanished, and has the danger become manifest?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
This too, monks, is a danger in relation to forms.
Furthermore, monks, suppose one were to see that same sister afflicted, suffering, gravely ill, lying fouled in her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by some and laid down by others.
What do you think, monks?
“Has that former beautiful appearance and luster vanished, and has the danger become manifest?
“It has, Bhante.
“This too, monks, is the danger in forms.”
Furthermore, monks, suppose one were to see that same woman’s body cast away in a charnel ground—
one day dead, or two days dead, or three days dead— swollen, discolored, and festering.
What do you think, monks?
‘That former beautiful appearance has vanished and the danger has become manifest,’ [he says].
‘Yes, venerable sir.
‘This too, monks, is the danger in forms.’
Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground,
being devoured by crows, or being devoured by hawks, or being devoured by vultures,
or being devoured by herons, or being devoured by dogs, or being devoured by tigers, or being devoured by leopards.
“Or it might be being devoured by jackals, or being devoured by various kinds of creatures.
What do you think, monks, has that former beautiful appearance vanished, and has the danger become manifest?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
This too, monks, is a danger in regard to forms.

Furthermore, monks, one might see that very same woman’s body cast away in a charnel ground—a skeleton with flesh and blood still adhering, bound together by sinews; or a skeleton devoid of flesh and smeared with blood.
A skeleton bound together by sinews, devoid of flesh and blood;
bones separated from their attachments and scattered in every direction—
the hand-bone in one place, the foot-bone in another, the ankle-bone in another, and the shin-bone in another.
One bone of the thigh with another, one bone of the hip with another, one bone of the rib with another,
one bone of the spine with another, one bone of the shoulder-blade with another, one bone of the neck with another, one bone of the jaw with another,
one tooth with another, and the skull with another. What do you think, monks, has that former beautiful appearance vanished and has the danger become manifest?
‘Yes, venerable sir.
This too, monks, is a danger in regard to forms.
Furthermore, monks, one might see that same sister’s body discarded in a charnel ground—
Bones white, resembling the color of a conch shell; bones heaped together, three or four years old; bones rotted and crumbled into dust.
What do you think, monks, has that former beautiful appearance vanished, and has the danger become manifest?
‘Yes, venerable sir.
This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms.
And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from forms?
“Monks, the removal of desire and lust for forms, the abandoning of desire and lust for forms—
this is the escape from forms. For whatever ascetics or brahmins, monks, do not understand as they really are the gratification of forms as gratification,
the danger of forms as danger, and the escape from forms as escape— they will certainly [not] themselves [fully understand] forms.”
Or that they will cause another to fully understand it for the sake of suchness, so that by practicing accordingly one will fully understand form—
this is impossible. But those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who understand form as it really is— as gratification in its gratification,
as danger in its danger, and as escape in its escape— they indeed [will understand it] by themselves.
Or they will fully understand form, or they will encourage others toward suchness so that, by practicing accordingly, one will fully understand form—this is possible.
And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in feelings?

Here, bhikkhus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

At whatever time, monks, a monk— quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states— enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion,
at that time he does not intend for his own affliction, nor does he intend for the affliction of others, nor does he intend for the affliction of both;
At that time, he experiences feeling that is entirely free from affliction.
Monks, I declare that the gratification of feelings is supreme when they are free from affliction.
Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk experiences internal serenity...

With the one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and accompanied by rapture and happiness, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna … [and so on] … Monks, at whatever time a monk, with the fading away of rapture, dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells happily”—he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. … [and so on] … Monks, at whatever time a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity. This is called the development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops this basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving, he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving. This is called the development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops this basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving, he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving. This is called the development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops this basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. This is called the development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops these four bases for psychic power, cultivated and made much of, for seven years, one of two fruits may be expected for him: either final knowledge here and now, or, if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return. Let alone seven years, monks, if a bhikkhu develops these four bases for psychic power … for six years … five years … four years … three years … two years … one year … seven months … six months … five months … four months … three months … two months … one month … half a month … for seven days, one of two fruits may be expected for him: either final knowledge here and now, or, if there is a trace of clinging left, non-return. Monks, if anyone should say: “I do not see even one other basis for psychic power that, when developed and made much of, leads so directly to the realization of supreme security from bondage as does this basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving,” about that person it should be said: “It is because he has not seen the range of the Tathāgata’s power, or he is a fool, or he speaks out of malice. Why is that? Because, monks, I do not see even one other basis for psychic power that, when developed and made much of, leads so directly to the realization of supreme security from bondage as does this basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: “We will develop the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, cultivated and made much of. It is in such a way that you should train yourselves. Monks, when a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, cultivated and made much of, he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. What states are these? Here, monks, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by desire and accompanied by effort; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by energy and accompanied by effort; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by mind and accompanied by effort; he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by examination and accompanied by effort. When he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by desire and accompanied by effort, his mind becomes concentrated, his defilements are abandoned, and he attains the destruction of the taints. When he develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, accompanied by energy … accompanied by mind … accompanied by examination and accompanied by effort, his mind becomes concentrated, his defilements are abandoned, and he attains the destruction of the taints. Or, if he desires: “May I wield the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and vanish; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though it were water; may I walk on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, may I travel in space like a bird; with my hand may I touch and stroke the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; may I exercise mastery with the body as far as the brahma world,” he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Or, if he desires: “May I, with the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, hear both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near,” he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Or, if he desires: “May I understand the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind. May I understand a mind affected by lust as affected by lust, and a mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust; may I understand a mind affected by hate as affected by hate, and a mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate; may I understand a mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion, and a mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion; may I understand a contracted mind as contracted, and a distracted mind as distracted; may I understand an exalted mind as exalted, and an unexalted mind as unexalted; may I understand a surpassed mind as surpassed, and an unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed; may I understand a concentrated mind as concentrated, and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; may I understand a liberated mind as liberated, and an unliberated mind as unliberated,” he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Or, if he desires: “May I recollect my manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, many eons of world-dissolution and evolution: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my life span; passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus may I recollect my manifold past lives in their modes and details,” he acquires whatever state realizable by direct knowledge that is attainable by right development of the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving. Or, if he desires: “May I, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, see beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understand how beings pass on according to their actions: ‘Truly, these beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong view, and undertook kamma based on wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook kamma based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, have
‘Dwelling in happiness,’ he enters and dwells in the third jhāna …pe… “At whatever time,
bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna,
which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.”
Having attained and dwelling in jhāna, at that time he does not intend for his own harm, nor does he intend for the harm of others,
nor does he intend for the harm of both;
at that time, he experiences only a feeling that is free from affliction.
"Bhikkhus, I say that the gratification in feelings is supreme non-affliction.
And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in feelings?
That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings."
And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from feelings?
That which is the removal of desire and lust for feelings, the abandoning of desire and lust for feelings—this is the escape from feelings.
For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, [regard] the gratification in feelings as gratification and the danger in feelings as danger...
Those who do not understand, as it truly is, the danger in what is dangerous and the escape from what is dangerous as an escape,
it is impossible that they will themselves fully understand feeling, or encourage another to practice in such a way that one practicing thus would fully understand feeling.
But as for those recluses or brahmins, bhikkhus, who [understand] the gratification of feelings as gratification...
“Those who understand, as they really are, the danger in what is dangerous and the escape from what is subject to escape—
they will indeed either fully understand feeling for themselves, or they will encourage another to practice in such a way that they will fully understand feeling; this is possible.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The third discourse, the Mahādukkhakkhandha Sutta, is finished.
